note: The Roman king who leads his spearmen against the "Assyrians" as far as the Euphrates, "a young Ares" who, "by his friend betrayed", falls "in the ranks", is Gordian III (r. 238–244), killed on campaign against Shapur I in his late teens. The friend is Philip, his praetorian prefect, who succeeds him in the next lines (13.21). The oracle names no one; it is read this way because of where it stands in the book's run of emperors and because of who follows. Compare Zosimus 1.19 and Zonaras 12.18, where Philip's plot kills him, and Shapur's own account, *Res Gestae* 6–7, where he falls in battle.
sources: D. S. Potter, *Prophecy and History in the Crisis of the Roman Empire: A Historical Commentary on the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle* (Oxford, 1990)

note: The "purple-loving warrior" who comes "out of Syria" with "his son, a Caesar", both bearing "the one name", is Philip the Arab (r. 244–249), from Roman Arabia, and his son Philip, made Caesar in 244. The oracle marks the name by the number of its first letter: "five hundred" is Φ, for Φίλιππος.
sources: D. S. Potter, *Prophecy and History in the Crisis of the Roman Empire: A Historical Commentary on the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle* (Oxford, 1990)
